questions.question: Differntiate between conditional branching and unconditional branching in AVR / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Conditional Branching - Branching occurs only when a specified condition is satisfied. It
  • depends on status flags such as Zero (Z), Carry (C), etc. Examples: BREQ, BRNE, BRCS. It
  • is used for decision-making and loop control.
  • Unconditional Branching - Branching occurs without checking any condition. It does not
  • depend on status flags. Examples: RJMP, JMP, IJMP. It is used to jump directly to another part
  • of the program. [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: Explain the procedure for generating a time delay using an AVR timer in Normal mode / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• In AVR microcontrollers, a time delay can be generated using a timer in Normal mode by
  • loading an initial value into the timer counter and waiting for it to overflow.
  • Select the timer: Choose Timer0, Timer1, or Timer2 depending on the required delay.
  • Configure Normal mode: Set the timer control register bits (WGM) to 0 to select Normal mode.
  • Set the pre -scaler: Select a suitable pre -scaler value to divide the CPU clock and obtain the
  • required timer frequency.
  • Load the initial count: Load the appropriate initial value into the timer counter register
  • (TCNTn). The timer increments with each timer clock pulse.
  • Wait for overflow: When the timer reaches its maximum value and rolls over to zero, the
  • overflow flag (TOVn) is set. Poll this flag or use an overflow interrupt. Clear the flag after
  • detecting the overflow.
  • Generate the delay: Calculate the delay from the timer tick duration and the number of counts.
  • Repeat the overflow process if a longer delay is required. [A] / [CO2]

questions.question: How do you configure an AVR port pin as an output to control an LED? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Select a port pin: Choose a pin, for example, PB0 of the AVR microcontroller.
  • Configure as output: Set the corresponding bit in the Data Direction Register (DDRB) to 1.
  • Turn ON the LED: Set the corresponding bit in the Port Register (PORTB) to 1.
  • Turn OFF the LED: Clear the corresponding bit in PORTB to 0.
  • Connect the LED: Connect the LED to the output pin through a current -limiting resistor to
  • prevent damage. An AVR port pin is configured as an output by setting its corresponding DDR
  • bit to 1. The LED is switched ON or OFF by setting or clearing the corresponding PORT bit.
  • [An] / [CO3]

questions.question: What are the main components of a microcontroller? Differentiate between a microprocessor and a microcontroller. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• The main components of a microcontroller are: CPU (Central Processing Unit) / Memory
  • / Input/Output (I/O) Ports / Timers/Counters / Communication Interfaces / Interrupt Controller
  • and Clock Circuit.
  • A microprocessor is mainly designed for general -purpose computing, whereas a
  • microcontroller integrates the CPU, memory and peripherals to control embedded applications.
  • Microprocessor - Mainly contains the CPU. Requires external memory and I/O interfaces.
  • Generally used in computers and high -performance computing systems. Usually consumes
  • more system power due to external components. Overall system cost is generally higher due to
  • additional components.
  • Microcontroller - Contains CPU, memory and peripherals on a single chip. Usually has built -
  • in memory and I/O peripherals. Generally used in embedded systems and control applications.
  • Usually offers lower system power consumption. Overall system cost is generally lower for
  • dedicated control tasks. [K] / [CO1]

questions.question: What is the function of the Enable (EN) pin of an LCD? / [CO3] [5x4 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• The Enable (EN) pin controls when the LCD accepts data or commands from the
  • microcontroller. The microcontroller places the command or data on the LCD data pins before
  • activating the EN pin. A pulse is applied to the EN pin to initiate the transfer of data or a
  • command. The LCD reads and latches the data or command, typically on the falling edge of
  • the EN pulse in common HD44780 -compatible LCDs. The EN pin synchronizes
  • communication between the A VR microcontroller and the LCD. The Enable (EN) pin is used
  • to control and synchronize the transfer of commands and data from the A VR microcontroller
  • to the LCD. [U] / [CO3]

questions.question: Draw and explain the block diagram of the AVR ATmega32 architecture. Describe the CPU, register, ALU, program memory, data memory and peripheral interfaces. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• CPU (Central Processing Unit) - 8-bit RISC processor / Executes instructions and controls all
  • operations / Uses a Harvard architecture with separate program and data memory.
  • Registers - Contains 32 general -purpose 8-bit registers (R0 –R31) / Used to store temporary
  • data and operands / Three 16-bit pointer registers: X, Y and Z.
  • ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) - Performs arithmetic and logical operations / Supports addition,
  • subtraction, AND, OR, XOR and comparison / Updates status flags in the Status Register
  • (SREG).
  • Program Memory - 32 KB Flash memory / Stores the program instructions / Non-volatile
  • memory.
  • Data Memory - 2 KB SRAM – stores temporary data and variables / 1 KB EEPROM – stores
  • data permanently / Also includes I/O registers for controlling peripherals.
  • Peripheral Interfaces - I/O ports: 32 programmable I/O pins (Ports A, B, C and D) / Three
  • timers/counters for timing and counting /10-bit, 8 -channel analog -to-digital converter /
  • USART, SPI and Two -Wire Interface (I²C -compatible) / Watchdog timer, interrupts and
  • analog comparator. [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: Explain the memory organization of ATmega32 with a neat diagram. Discuss Program Counter, Program Memory, Data Memory, SRAM, EEPROM, and Stack. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• The ATmega32 is an 8-bit AVR RISC microcontroller that uses a Harvard architecture, in
  • which program memory and data memory are separate. It has three main types of memory:
  • Flash program memory, SRAM, and EEPROM. Similar diagram can be used.
  • The Program Counter is a 16-bit register that holds the address of the next instruction to be
  • fetched from program memory. It automatically increments as instructions are executed.
  • During jump, call, interrupt, or return operations, its value may change to the required address.
  • ATmega32 has 32 KB of Flash program memory . It stores the program instructions and
  • constants. It is non -volatile, so data remains stored even when the power is switched off. It
  • supports in-system programming and can be reprogrammed.
  • The data memory contains the register file, I/O registers, and internal SRAM. 32 general-
  • purpose registers: R0 –R31, each 8 bits wide. 64 I/O register locations: used to control
  • peripherals and microcontroller functions. Extended I/O locations are also available in the
  • ATmega32's data address space.
  • ATmega32 contains 2 KB of internal SRAM. It is volatile memory, meaning its contents are
  • lost when power is removed. It stores variables, temporary results, function parameters, and
  • local variables during program execution.
  • ATmega32 has 1 KB of EEPROM. It is non-volatile memory that retains data without power.
  • It stores user settings, calibration values, and other data that must be preserved. It can be
  • electrically erased and rewritten by the program.
  • The stack is a memory area located in SRAM and follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out)
  • principle. The Stack Pointer (SP) is a 16 -bit register that points to the top of the stack. The
  • stack stores return addresses during function calls and interrupts, as well as temporary data and
  • saved registers. [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: Describe the steps involved in transmitting a character and explain the role of the UDRE and TXC flags. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• The important registers and flags involved are: UDR (USART Data Register): Holds the
  • character to be transmitted. UDRE (USART Data Register Empty): Indicates that the UDR can
  • accept new data. TXC (Transmit Complete): Indicates that the entire character has been
  • transmitted, including the stop bit. Steps Involved in Transmitting a Character:
  • Initialize USART: Set the baud rate using UBRRH and UBRRL, configure the frame format
  • using UCSRC, and enable the transmitter using TXEN in UCSRB.
  • Check UDRE: Read the UDRE flag in UCSRA. If UDRE = 0, wait until the data register
  • becomes empty.
  • Load the character: When UDRE = 1, write the character into UDR.
  • Transmit the character: The USART transfers the data to its shift register and sends it serially
  • through TXD, including the start bit, data bits, optional parity bit, and stop bit.
  • Check TXC: Wait until TXC = 1 if the program needs to confirm that the complete character
  • has left the transmitter.
  • UDRE is a status flag in the UCSRA register. It becomes 1 when the USART data register is
  • ready to accept new data. It becomes 0 when new data is written to UDR, until the register
  • becomes available again. It allows the program to load the next character without overwriting
  • data that has not yet been transferred. It is useful for continuous or back -to-back character
  • transmission.
  • TXC is a status flag in the UCSRA register. It is set to 1 when the entire frame in the transmit
  • shift register has been shifted out and no new data is waiting in the transmit buffer. It indicates
  • that transmission is physically complete, including the stop bit. It is useful when disabling the
  • transmitter, switching a half-duplex communication line, or ensuring the last character has been
  • sent before proceeding. TXC is cleared by hardware when its documented clearing conditions
  • occur; on the ATmega32, it can also be cleared by writing a logic 1 to the TXC bit.
  • [K] / [CO2]
